title: He Has Risen: Emmaus, the Upper Room, and the Ascension
summary: On the first day of the week the women find Jesus' tomb empty and hear from two angels that he has risen. That afternoon the risen Jesus walks unrecognized with two disciples to Emmaus, explains the Scriptures about himself, and is recognized in the breaking of bread. He then appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and feet, eats before them, opens their minds to the Scriptures, commissions them as witnesses to all nations, and is carried up into heaven from near Bethany.
story: Everything in Luke has been moving toward Jerusalem, and here the story reaches its goal. The Jesus who was crucified and buried in chapter 23 is alive, and the chapter moves in a single day from confusion and grief to worship and great joy. The key to the whole chapter is Scripture: Jesus shows that his suffering and rising were written in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and that the next chapter of the story is the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. Luke ends where he began, in the temple, with people praising God. His second volume, Acts, picks up exactly here, retelling the ascension (and making clear that the appearances continued over forty days, Acts 1:3) and following the witnesses from Jerusalem to Rome.
historical:
The chapter's events fall on the Sunday after the Passover at which Jesus was crucified. Passover week had filled Jerusalem with pilgrims, and the crucifixion took place on the Friday, the day of Preparation before the Sabbath (23:54). The year is not fixed, but working from Pilate's and Caiaphas's terms of office, the fifteenth year of Tiberius (3:1), and the years in which Passover fell near a Friday, most scholars favor AD 30 or AD 33. Pontius Pilate governed Judea as Roman prefect from about AD 26 to 36, and Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36. Both are known outside the Bible: Pilate from Josephus, Philo, and an inscription found at Caesarea in 1961, Caiaphas from Josephus.

Emmaus has several candidate sites, and none is certain. Emmaus Nicopolis (modern Imwas), a well-known town of the period, lies about 19 miles from Jerusalem, which fits the manuscript reading of 160 stadia but makes the walk there and back in one evening hard. El-Qubeibeh, honored as Emmaus since the Crusades, and Abu Ghosh lie nearer the seven miles of most manuscripts. Motza, a few miles west of the city, is often linked with the Emmaus where Josephus says Vespasian settled veterans after the Jewish war. The church confesses that Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day, and Luke tells it as an event in history, set in real places among people who can be named, Cleopas among them. The earliest written witness is Paul's summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, from the mid-50s, which passes on a tradition he had received earlier still.
cultural:
Jewish burial customs called for anointing the body with spices and perfumes, which the women had prepared but could not bring on the Sabbath. Emmaus was a village about seven miles (literally sixty stadia) from Jerusalem, and its exact location is uncertain. Hospitality meant inviting a traveler to stay as evening fell. At the meal, the stranger takes the host's role, blessing and breaking the bread, and in that familiar act they know him.

The disciples' first fear, that they were seeing a spirit, reflects a widespread ancient belief in ghosts, the shades of the dead. Jesus answers it directly: a spirit does not have flesh and bones. Many Jews expected a resurrection of all the righteous at the end of the age, not the resurrection of one person in the middle of history, which is part of why the disciples were so slow to grasp what had happened. The phrase the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms names the three parts of the Hebrew Scriptures, the Psalms standing for the Writings.
literary: The chapter is a sequence of three scenes on one day: the empty tomb at dawn (verses 1 to 12), the road to Emmaus in the afternoon (verses 13 to 35), and the appearance to the gathered disciples in the evening, followed by the ascension (verses 36 to 53). Each scene moves from perplexity to understanding, and each turns on remembering or opening. The women remember his words; the Emmaus disciples' eyes are opened; the disciples' minds are opened to the Scriptures. The Emmaus story is a masterpiece of irony, with the risen Jesus hearing his own story told as a tragedy by people who do not recognize him. The chapter echoes the beginning of the Gospel, which also opened in the temple with worship. Several phrases are missing from the Western text, chiefly Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies: ‘of the Lord Jesus’ (verse 3), “He is not here; He has risen!” (verse 6), all of verse 12, Jesus' greeting of peace (verse 36), all of verse 40, “and was carried up into heaven” (verse 51), and the disciples' worship (verse 52). Westcott and Hort (1881) called these ‘Western non-interpolations’ and printed the shorter text, judging that here alone the Western copies had kept the original. The papyrus P75, copied around AD 200 and published in 1961, contains every one of them, and since its discovery most scholars accept them as original. In verse 13 Codex Sinaiticus reads 160 stadia (about 19 miles) instead of 60.

outline.t: Known in the breaking of the bread
Jesus appears to the disciples in the flesh
The Scriptures opened and the witnesses commissioned

doctrines.note: Jesus' resurrection is bodily: he has flesh and bones, bears the wounds of the cross, and eats fish. It is the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to his people and the ground of Christian hope that death will not have the last word over the body or the world.

The risen Jesus teaches that all of Scripture, Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, speaks of him. He does not replace the Old Testament but interprets it, and the church has read it in his light ever since.

Repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. The disciples are witnesses, and they are to wait for the promise of the Father, power from on high, which Acts will describe as the gift of the Holy Spirit.

words.note: Egeirō, to raise or rise. The angels say “He is not here; He has risen!” The verb here is passive in form and can be rendered he has been raised, pointing to God as the one who raised him. The New Testament speaks both of Jesus rising and of God raising him.

Diermēneuō, to interpret or explain thoroughly. Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Jesus explained what was written in all the Scriptures about himself. It is built on the same root as the English word hermeneutics, the discipline of interpretation, and it makes the risen Jesus the church's first teacher of how to read the Old Testament.

Martus, witness. “You are witnesses of these things.” A witness testifies to what he has seen and heard, which is why the resurrection appearances matter. Because so many early witnesses died for their testimony, the word later came to mean martyr.

christ: This chapter shows Jesus as the living Lord, the same Jesus who was crucified, now raised in a real and transformed body. His wounds are still there; he eats, speaks, and blesses, yet he appears and disappears and is not always recognized at first. He interprets Israel's Scriptures as a single story that runs through the Christ's suffering to his glory. He sends his disciples to all nations and promises the Spirit. He blesses them with lifted hands, like a priest, and is carried into heaven, and they worship him, the right response to one who is Lord. The resurrection declares that Jesus' death was not defeat, that his claims were true, and that the new creation has begun.

hard.q: Did the resurrection really happen, or can it be explained another way?
hard.a:
The church confesses that Jesus rose bodily from the dead, and Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). The skeptic's case deserves its strongest form first. Gerd Lüdemann, in The Resurrection of Jesus (1994), argued that Jesus' body decayed and that the appearances were visions: Peter's born of grief and guilt after his denial, Paul's of inner conflict, and the group experiences a kind of shared ecstasy. Bart Ehrman, in How Jesus Became God (2014), doubts that Jesus received an honorable burial in a known tomb, since Rome often left the crucified unburied, and holds that some disciples sincerely saw visions that convinced them he was alive. Dale Allison, himself a Christian, gathered in Resurrecting Jesus (2005) modern reports of visions of the dead, some seen by several people at once, which weakens the familiar reply that hallucinations are always private. The skeptic can also point to real discrepancies among the accounts: Mark has one young man at the tomb, Matthew one angel, Luke two men, John two angels; the lists of women differ; Matthew and Mark point to Galilee, while Luke keeps every appearance in and near Jerusalem; and Luke seems to set the ascension on Easter day here but forty days later in Acts 1.

Christian scholars answer in turn. N. T. Wright, in The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), argues that first-century Jews would not have called visions of a dead man resurrection, a word that meant a body raised, and that only an empty tomb together with appearances explains why they did. Michael Licona, in The Resurrection of Jesus (2010), argues by historians' criteria that resurrection best explains the facts most scholars grant. Both note that the early tradition in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 lists group appearances, that women as first witnesses are an odd thing to invent, and that independent accounts commonly differ in detail while agreeing on the core: the tomb found empty on the first day by women, and Jesus seen alive. Many who reject the resurrection do so because they judge that the dead do not rise, a conviction the evidence cannot settle by itself. Luke leaves the reader where he left the Emmaus disciples: with the Scriptures, the testimony of witnesses, and an invitation to recognize the risen one.

questions: The Emmaus disciples said, “But we were hoping.” Where have your hopes in God seemed to end in disappointment, and how might this story speak to that?
Jesus showed his wounds after he rose. What does it mean that the risen Christ still bears the marks of the cross?
The disciples' hearts burned as Jesus opened the Scriptures. What would help you read the Old Testament as a book that speaks of him?
